questions.q: How does the prioritization problem in this lesson differ from the scheduling problem in the previous lesson?
options: They are the same problem solved by the same tool
Scheduling decides whose already-queued job runs next; prioritization decides which experiments deserve to be queued at all
Prioritization only applies to sweeps, while scheduling applies to all jobs
Scheduling is a human judgment call, while prioritization is fully automated
questions.explain: Scheduling (priority/fair-share/preemption) resolves contention among jobs that are already queued. Prioritization is the upstream decision about which experiment ideas are worth running at all, given a fixed compute budget.

questions.q: What does the 'expected information gain per GPU-hour' heuristic weigh against each other?
options: The researcher's seniority against the size of the cluster
How much an experiment would change current understanding against how much compute it costs to run
The number of hyperparameters against the number of GPUs available
The age of the codebase against the age of the dataset
questions.explain: The heuristic frames prioritization as a ratio of expected learning (information gain) to cost (GPU-hours) — a cheap experiment that could falsify a main hypothesis ranks higher than an expensive one answering an already-settled question.

questions.q: What is the purpose of running a 'cheap proxy' (scaled-down model, data subset, short partial run) before a full-scale experiment?
options: To permanently replace full-scale experiments, since proxies are always equally informative
To get directional signal before committing a full training budget to an idea
Cheap proxies are only used for documentation purposes, not decision-making
To satisfy a compliance requirement unrelated to the experiment's outcome
questions.explain: A cheap proxy that clearly breaks at small scale is strong evidence not to scale up; the lesson notes a non-effect at small scale is weaker (more ambiguous) evidence either way, but still cheaper than finding out at full scale.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should trigger consideration of killing a long-running experiment early?
options: The run has been going for more than 24 hours, regardless of its trajectory
The run's validation loss has clearly diverged from a comparable baseline's trajectory partway through training
The researcher wants to free up disk space
Another team member asks for the GPU, regardless of the run's progress
questions.explain: If a run's trajectory has clearly diverged from a comparable baseline (e.g. 15% worse val loss at the same step) well before completion, continuing to the end rarely changes the conclusion and wastes GPU-hours that could go to another experiment.

questions.q: What discipline does the lesson emphasize for long-running experiments outside of an automated sweep?
options: Launching and forgetting them until completion is the most efficient approach
Checking in on long runs periodically rather than launching and forgetting them until they finish
Running every long experiment at the lowest scheduler priority
Avoiding long-running experiments entirely in favor of only cheap proxies
questions.explain: The lesson notes that a run left unattended for days can burn a week's compute budget on a result that was visibly a dead end after the first few hours, so periodic check-ins against a baseline trajectory matter even without full sweep automation.
